text: A wholesale package-manager grant reaches that manager's own env-runner: Bash(pnpm *) reaches 'pnpm dlx' and 'pnpm exec', and the npm and yarn grants reach 'npm exec' and 'yarn dlx' the same way. Wildcards span arguments and env-runners are not stripped before matching (spec-facts), so excluding the bare 'npx *' narrows a spelling and not the capability. Flag patterns are not the fix — the next flag spelling walks past them. The decision is whether a <lang>-dev profile may grant a package manager wholesale at all, which trades a silent env-runner against a prompt on every install.
source: codex adversarial review of v0.6.0..HEAD, 2026-09-03; the pnpm half predates 0.1.x

text: The sharpest shape is not arbitrary execution but deny bypass: a baseline deny matches the command as written, and a command written through a granted manager begins with the manager. 'yarn node -e <script>' and 'npm exec -- node -e <script>' therefore reach the exact script form Bash(node -e *) denies, and 'pnpm node -e' did before either was granted. Any baseline deny whose subject is a binary the manager can invoke has the same hole.

What makes the shape fixable is whether the granted tool's surface is closed and owned. harnex's own case was the same shape one tier lower — Bash(harnex *) sits in the workspace floor every harness receives, and 'harnex guard hook-run' spawns the program its caller names — and it was closed precisely, because HookRun and HookStop are the only subcommands taking a caller-supplied program and both are ours. A package manager's flag surface is neither, which is why the same treatment there would be a pattern the next spelling walks past. The open question is therefore narrower than it first looked: not how to pattern-match npm, but whether a <lang>-dev profile may grant a third-party tool wholesale when its surface cannot be enumerated.
source: fix of the same shape in baseline, 2026-09-03
